title: Next.js 16 makes caching explicit with use cache
excerpt: Next.js 16 replaces implicit caching with the use cache directive, letting developers decide what, when, and how to cache.
body:
A recent upgrade to Next.js 16 swapped the framework’s hidden caching rules for an explicit `use cache` directive. In earlier releases a plain `fetch` could end up cached forever, or a route segment could become static without any visible hint.

The result was production pages serving data that was hours old, and developers scrambling to add or remove `unstable_cache` wrappers. The new model forces you to name what you cache, decide how long it lives, and give it a tag you can clear later.

In the following sections you’ll see which old mechanisms disappear, how to cache at the function and component level, and how `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` let you control freshness. By the end you’ll have a clear migration path and a mental model that works the same for database calls, HTTP requests, and React Server Components.

## How `use cache` replaces old mechanisms

Next.js 15 and earlier relied on three separate patterns:

* `unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, options)`, a wrapper that memoized the result of a data-fetching function. The API was marked unstable and never graduated.
* Fetch-specific cache options, passing `{ next: { revalidate: 3600 } }` to `fetch` stored the HTTP response for an hour. Only fetch calls benefitted from this.
* Implicit route caching, the compiler inspected a route segment and, if it found no dynamic calls (cookies, headers, `searchParams`), it prerendered the segment as static. Any child that called a dynamic function forced the whole segment to become dynamic, a decision hidden from the developer.

All three are gone. Adding `use cache` to a function or component tells the framework to store the return value. The cache key is automatically built from the function’s arguments and any captured variables, so there is no need for a separate wrapper. Because the directive works everywhere, you no longer need fetch-only options or heuristic route analysis. The result is a single, predictable caching model.

## Function-level and component-level caching

The directive can be placed on any async function that returns data, or on a React Server Component that returns JSX. When the function is invoked, Next.js runs it once, stores the result, and returns the cached value on subsequent calls with the same arguments.

```js
use cache
async function getProducts() {
  // fetch data
}
```

In this example the framework caches the result of `getProducts`. If the function receives parameters, each distinct set of arguments becomes a separate cache entry. Closures are also part of the key, so a function that closes over a request-specific value will not collide with another request.

Component-level caching works the same way. Wrapping a Server Component with `use cache` means the entire rendered tree is stored. Subsequent renders that hit the same cache key skip the component’s execution entirely, which can cut server-side rendering time dramatically.

Because the cache key generation is automatic, you avoid the manual key strings that `unstable_cache` required. The only thing you need to add for control is `cacheLife` and `cacheTag`.

## Controlling freshness with `cacheLife` and `cacheTag`

`cacheLife` defines how long a cached entry stays valid. The function accepts a predefined profile such as `'seconds'`, `'minutes'`, `'hours'`, or `'days'`. Calling it after `use cache` attaches the lifetime to that cache entry.

```js
cacheLife('hours')
```

The above line tells Next.js to expire the cached result after one hour. If you need a custom duration you can pass a number of seconds, but the profile strings cover most use cases and keep the code readable.

Invalidation is handled by `cacheTag`. By assigning one or more tags to a cache entry, you can clear all entries that share the tag on demand. This is useful when a downstream data source changes and you need to purge related caches.

```js
cacheTag(['products'])
```

When the product catalog updates, a server-side mutation can call `revalidateTag('products')` (the API that clears tags) and every cache entry that was created with `cacheTag(['products'])` is removed immediately. The next request will recompute `getProducts` and store a fresh result.

Together, `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` give you two levers: time-based expiration for predictable staleness, and event-based invalidation for when data changes out of band. The source notes that this combination replaces the older `fetch` `revalidate` option and the manual invalidation logic developers built around `unstable_cache`.

## The takeaway

Next.js 16 removes implicit caching and three legacy APIs, replacing them with a single `use cache` directive. Mark a function or component with `use cache`, set its lifetime with `cacheLife`, and give it a tag for on-demand clearing with `cacheTag`. The result is predictable, uniform caching across data sources and UI rendering.
